title: Darkening a photo is not the same as driving at night
paper_title: Questioning Post-hoc Image Corruptions as a Proxy for Environmental Variation in Autonomous Driving
date_note: Information Society 2026 multiconference, Ljubljana, early October 2026 (proceedings Vol. 1, pp. 60-63); exact day approximate
summary: A short guide to the post-hoc corruptions paper: a darkening filter and a simulated night look alike but test a driving agent very differently. Full write-up on the LANCER page.
cta: Read the full write-up on the LANCER page

body.p: This paper belongs to LANCER, my project at the University of Ljubljana on autonomous navigation in complex environments using reinforcement learning. A part of that work is about testing: how do we know a camera-driven car will cope with night, fog or rain?

The common shortcut is to take recorded footage and damage it with image filters, such as darkening it or adding a fog-like veil, then see how badly the vision network copes. It is cheap, but it assumes the filtered picture stands in for the real condition. We checked that assumption in a driving simulator that can produce night and fog in two ways: by filtering the finished picture, and by changing the lighting and air in the scene before it is rendered.

figure.alt: Two rows of frames: with simulated night the car leaves the road, while with the matched darkening filter it completes the run; for fog the physical condition and its filter look and behave alike.
figure.caption: The same road, agent and random seed. The simulated night puts the car off the road. The filter that matches it does not.

body.p: Fog passed the test: the real fog and its filter agree at every strength. Night did not. At a picture change of 38 grey levels, the simulated night cost nine independently trained agents 0.51 of their driving performance, while the matched darkening filter cost nothing measurable. All nine agents agreed (p = 0.004). Training with filters did not help either: an agent trained that way did slightly worse against physical conditions (8.68 laps out of ten, against 9.05 without it), while training on re-rendered conditions completed every lap.

So whether a filter is a fair stand-in depends on the physics of the condition it imitates. The details, including a distance-based test we tried and what it can and cannot tell you, are on the project page.
